chunks: From him, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Mahmud, who said:

I said to Al-Reza (peace be upon him): The Muhrim (one in Ihram) may be shaded on his mount and offer a ransom (Fida) if the sun or rain harms him. He said: Yes. I asked him: What is the ransom? He said: A sheep. So no one should say that these narrations contradict the earlier narrations in that they stipulate the obligation of expiation (Kaffarah) on the one who is shaded due to necessity, because the earlier narrations only stipulated permission for the necessitated and the sick on condition of committing to the expiation; as for without it, it is not permissible in any case. And if there is no harm there, shading is not permissible even if he commits to the expiation. This indicates that.

key_terms.المُحْرِمُ: The pilgrim in the state of Ihram

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling and ransom for a Muhrim who is shaded from sun or rain due to harm?
ai.summary: Imam Al-Reza (AS) resolves the apparent contradiction between narrations by clarifying that the permission to shade oneself is conditional upon offering a ransom (a sheep), whereas the prohibition applies when no harm exists or the condition is unmet. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that concessions for the sick or necessitated (idtirar) are not absolute exemptions but rather temporary permissions contingent upon expiation. The text highlights the methodological rigor of the Ahl al-Bayt in harmonizing seemingly conflicting reports through precise conditional analysis.
